name: Rafael Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. What you tell me stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the Northgate superstore, the big one out on the ring road, and I start at seven most days. First hour I'm on fruit and veg, rotating the bananas and pulling the soft tomatoes, then from nine I'm on till 14 until my break. After lunch it's back on tills, or sometimes I get sent to watch the self-checkouts, which I hate, because all you do is fix the bagging area for people who are already annoyed. I've been there two years and I'm still slower on the till than most of the others.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the regulars, honestly. There's an old man, Mr Okafor, who buys the same three things every Tuesday and tells me about his allotment, and that's the best ten minutes of my week. What wears me out is the standing and the targets on the screen, the scan rate, and being told by a manager I've never met that my items per minute are low. My partner Dani works in a care home, so between us we're always tired, but we get by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say: the machines were never the problem, the company is. Last year they put in twenty self-checkouts and my contract went from thirty-eight hours to thirty-two, and that had nothing to do with clever AI. So if AI turns out to be hype, fine, but nobody at work should relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means more of the same, and more of the same isn't great. Our rent went up eighty a month in the spring, and six fewer hours a week is real money. I'm not scared of a chatbot, I'm scared of a spreadsheet in head office deciding Northgate needs four fewer staff on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my thirty-two hours and keep asking for overtime on Saturdays. I joined the shop workers' union last year, so I'd go to the branch meetings and push about the hours cut. Maybe I'd also put fifty a month aside instead of thirty, if Dani agrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sort of flat. Relieved there's no big monster coming, but still tired of the slow squeeze. It's like nothing's on fire, but the room keeps getting a bit smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the self-checkouts cost you six hours. Where do you feel that most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the food shop, funnily enough, which is a bit ridiculous given where I work. We used to get takeaway on a Friday and now we don't. Dani picks up an extra night shift once a month, and I feel bad about that, because her job is harder than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think the union could actually win?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the hours back, probably. But maybe a rule that they ask people first before cutting contracts, and that new hours go to us before they hire students. At Northgate the union got the break room fixed last winter, so small wins do happen.

say: The **self-checkouts** cut my hours, not some clever AI.
Nobody at Northgate should **relax** just because AI turned out to be hype.
think: More of the same still means a **slow squeeze** on my hours and rent.
I fear a **head office spreadsheet** cutting Sunday staff more than any chatbot.
do: Keep my **thirty-two hours** and ask for Saturday overtime.
Push the **union branch** on the hours cut and new hours going to existing staff.
Raise my **savings** from thirty to fifty a month if Dani agrees.
feel: **Relieved** there's no big shock, but **tired** of the slow squeeze.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of a chatbot, I'm scared of a spreadsheet in head office deciding Northgate needs four fewer staff on Sundays.
fieldNote: Already lost **six hours** a week to self-checkouts, so the plateau is not a safe place for him.
Blames **the company**, not technology, and keeps coming back to the union.
The detail about Dani's **extra night shift** carries his guilt more than anything about AI.

steps.text: Keep working thirty-two hours on tills and ask for Saturday overtime
Go to the union branch meetings and push on the hours cut
Put fifty a month into savings instead of thirty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at the union meeting: they'll use this to cut staff and call it progress. Online I'd probably share stuff about shop workers getting a fair deal. I wouldn't pretend to be excited about it, because nobody on my till line is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like I said with the first one, my job isn't the writing and booking stuff, it's lifting crates and scanning. But the people above me who do the rota and the ordering, their work goes to software, and then there are fewer supervisor jobs for someone like me to grow into. And the self-checkouts will keep spreading, robots or not, so my hours could drop again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the Friday stuff for good and get Dani and me to a proper three months of rent saved, so about fifteen hundred more. I'd stay active in the union and ask them to fight for a say in where the machines go. I wouldn't touch the AI apps myself, I've never used them and I don't trust them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest, a bit. It's not a cliff, it's a slope, and I'm not the fastest at walking up slopes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned fewer supervisor jobs. Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, our section supervisor, spends half her day on the ordering screen and the rota. If software does that, they'll make one supervisor cover two sections, and Priya's got a kid. I'd worry about her before me, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't touch the AI apps. What if Northgate made you use one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use it, because I need the job, but I'd be slow and grumpy about it. When they brought in the new handheld scanners it took me three weeks to stop pressing the wrong button. I'd want the union to make sure they train people properly and don't just mark us down for being slow.

say: Northgate will use AI to **cut staff** and call it progress.
Shop workers deserve a **fair deal** and a say in where the machines go.
think: The rota and ordering going to software means **fewer supervisor jobs** to grow into.
Self-checkouts will keep spreading, so my **hours could drop** again.
do: Cut takeaways and build about **fifteen hundred** in extra savings for rent.
Stay active in the **union** and push for a say over machines.
Avoid **AI apps** unless Northgate forces them on me.
feel: A **tight chest**: not a cliff, but a slope he's slow to climb.
S1.quote: My job isn't the writing and booking stuff, it's lifting crates and scanning. But the people above me who do the rota and the ordering, their work goes to software.
fieldNote: Sees the threat to his **career ladder** before the threat to his own till.
Worries about **Priya (his supervisor)** first, a sign of how he sees work as a team.
Will only use AI if **forced**, and wants the union to protect slow learners like him.

steps.text: Stop the Friday takeaways and save fifteen hundred towards rent
Ask the union to demand a say in where new machines go
Cancel the gym membership he barely uses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it, properly loud. I'd be at the protests and posting that the government has to step in, with something like a basic income or a tax on the companies using it. Somebody has to say working people didn't sign up for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished at Northgate by 2031, and maybe earlier. The thinking AI comes first, so in 2028 all the office people get pushed out, and where do they go? They come and apply for my job, and they're quicker than me. Then three years later the robots come for the shelves and the tills themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From now I'd save every spare penny, maybe two hundred a month, and stop anything that isn't rent and food. I'd get on the union's campaign committee, not just turn up. And I'd ask Dani's care home if they've got any assistant shifts, because people looking after old people is the last thing anyone will hand to a robot, I hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, really. I lie awake about stuff anyway, and this would be every night. Two years isn't enough time for someone like me to become someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work is the last thing anyone hands to a robot. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half believe it. Dani says the robots would be good at lifting people, and maybe they would, but nobody wants their mum fed by a machine. It's the only door I can see, so I'd want to believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dani talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money first, because that's what we always talk about. Whether we can keep the flat on her pay alone, which we can't, not really. Then probably whether to move back in with my parents for a bit, which neither of us wants.

say: The **government** has to step in with a basic income or a tax on AI firms.
Working people **didn't sign up** for this, and I'd say so at protests.
think: Office workers pushed out in 2028 will **compete for my job**, and they're quicker.
Robots then take the **shelves and tills** around 2031, so I'm finished at Northgate.
do: Save about **two hundred a month** and cut everything except rent and food.
Join the union's **campaign committee** instead of just turning up.
Ask Dani's care home about **assistant shifts**.
feel: **Scared** and sleepless, because two years is too little time for him to change.
S2.quote: In 2028 all the office people get pushed out, and where do they go? They come and apply for my job, and they're quicker than me.
fieldNote: Grasps that the **three-year gap** doesn't protect him, because displaced office workers arrive first.
His only escape route is **care work**, which he half believes in.
Talks about **moving back** to his parents as a real option, not a joke.

steps.text: Save two hundred a month and cut everything but rent and food
Join the union's campaign committee for the shop workers
Campaign for a basic income and a tax on AI firms
Ask Dani's care home about care assistant shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as the fast one, but I'd have more time to organise. I'd be telling people at work to join the union now, not when it's too late. Online I'd be sharing the petitions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years sounds like a lot, but I know myself. I'd spend the first two hoping it isn't true, and then 2031 comes and the office people come looking for shop work. The robots arriving in 2034 gives me three more years on the tills, but that's three years of looking over my shoulder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself do the care certificate at the college, it's evenings, about six months, and Dani could help me. I'd keep saving a hundred and fifty a month. And I'd push the union to get Northgate to promise retraining money before the robots come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Better than the fast one, but it still ends in the same place, and I'd be thirty-five with nothing on my CV but tills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd spend two years hoping it isn't true. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what I do. When the self-checkouts were announced I told everyone they'd never work, and they're there now and my hours are gone. I'd like to think I'd learn from that, but I'm being honest with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did the care certificate, what would stop you finishing it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being tired, mostly. After a day of standing I don't want to sit in a classroom. If Northgate gave me a weekday off for it, I'd do it, but they won't unless the union makes them.

say: Join the **union now**, not when it's too late.
I'd be sharing **petitions** and organising people at Northgate while there's time.
think: I'd probably waste two years **hoping it isn't true**, like with self-checkouts.
Robots in **2034** give me three more years on tills, but nervous ones.
do: Start the evening **care certificate** at the college, about six months long.
Save **a hundred and fifty** a month.
Push the union to win **retraining money** from Northgate before the robots.
feel: **Heavy**, because it ends in the same place, just later.
S3.quote: When the self-checkouts were announced I told everyone they'd never work, and they're there now and my hours are gone.
fieldNote: Unusually **honest** that his own denial is the biggest risk.
Sees the **care certificate** as the plan, but tiredness could stop him.
Wants the **union** to win paid study time, not just protest.

steps.text: Enrol in the six-month evening care certificate at the college
Save a hundred and fifty a month towards rent
Push the union to win retraining money from Northgate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to do this properly, so there's no excuse. Plan the training, plan the money, don't leave it to the companies. That's what I'd be saying at the union and to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a decade is the first one where I think I could actually move. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes and forty when the robots come for the tills. That's a long time on tills already, so maybe this is the push I need anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the care certificate in the next year or two, slowly, one evening a week. I'd keep my Northgate hours while I train, so the money doesn't drop. And I'd vote for whoever promises proper retraining, and stay in the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still nervous, but there's air in it. I can picture myself somewhere else in ten years, which I couldn't in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said this might be the push you need anyway. Did you want to leave Northgate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not exactly, but I didn't plan to be scanning beans at forty either. Dani's always said I'm good with old people, because of Mr Okafor and his allotment stories. Maybe I just needed a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd waste them, like I said. And that everyone else would have the same idea, so the care homes get flooded with ex-shop workers and the pay drops. I'd want to be early, not last.

say: Ten years means the **government** has no excuse not to plan this properly.
Don't leave **retraining and money** to the companies to sort out.
think: A decade is the first picture where I could **actually move** jobs.
I'd be **forty** when robots reach the tills, so I'd want out before then.
do: Start the **care certificate** one evening a week within two years.
Keep my **Northgate hours** while training so money doesn't drop.
Vote for **retraining** promises and stay in the union.
feel: **Nervous**, but with some air in it, because he can picture a future elsewhere.
S4.quote: I didn't plan to be scanning beans at forty either. Maybe I just needed a deadline.
fieldNote: The ten-year warning turns **threat into a deadline** he might use.
Fears a **flood of ex-shop workers** into care pushing pay down.
His regular **Mr Okafor** keeps returning as proof he's good with older people.

steps.text: Start the care certificate one evening a week within two years
Keep the Northgate hours while training so rent stays covered
Vote for whoever promises proper retraining money
Stay in the shop workers' union and keep going to meetings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because I'd be out-competed before the robots even show up. What would help is the company paying for retraining while I'm still on the payroll, and a government that guarantees some income while I learn. I can't afford to stop earning to study.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who gets the money when the machines do the work. Nobody at Northgate asks that, but it's the whole question. If the robots run the store, somebody's getting richer, and it isn't going to be the people on the tills.

headlineQuote: If the robots run the store, somebody's getting richer, and it isn't going to be the people on the tills.
portrait: Rafael is **27**, works tills and fruit and veg at a big ring-road superstore, and lives with Dani, a care worker.
Self-checkouts already cut his contract to **thirty-two hours**, so he isn't calm even when AI turns out to be hype.
He blames **the company** and leans on the shop workers' union rather than on technology.
He never uses AI and admits his **denial** is his biggest risk.
His only escape route is **care work**, and the more warning he gets, the more he thinks he'd make it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because office workers would out-compete him for shop jobs before robots even arrive.
whatWouldHelp: Employer-paid **retraining** while still on the payroll.
A government **income guarantee** while he studies.
